tips.title: Equilibrium means equal rates
tips.body: Equilibrium is reached when the **forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate**. It does **not** mean equal amounts of reactants and products — only that neither amount is changing any more.

tips.title: It needs a closed system
tips.body: Equilibrium is only reached **in apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products**. If a gas can leave, the reverse reaction runs out of material and the system never balances.

tips.title: The system counteracts the change
tips.body: **Le Chatelier's principle**: if a system at equilibrium has a condition changed, **the system responds to counteract the change**. Add something and it is used up; heat it and the system absorbs heat; squeeze it and it takes up less space.

tips.title: Pressure: count the molecules
tips.body: An **increase in pressure** shifts the equilibrium towards the side with the **smaller number of molecules**, as shown by the symbol equation. If both sides have the **same** number, pressure has **no effect** at all.

tips.title: Heating favours the endothermic direction
tips.body: Raise the temperature and the system **absorbs** the extra heat, so the **endothermic** direction is favoured. For an exothermic forward reaction, heating therefore makes **less** product — which is the trade-off at the heart of the Haber process.

why.matters:
Most reactions you meet go one way and stop when something runs out. A **reversible** one does not: the products react back, and what you are left with is a **balance** between two reactions running at the same rate in opposite directions.

That changes the question. You can no longer ask what the reaction gives you, only where the balance sits — and **Le Chatelier's principle** is the one rule for moving it. Every industrial process that never finishes is tuned with it.

examples.title: The blue crystals that go white and come back
examples.body:
Heat blue copper sulfate crystals and they turn white, giving off water. Add the water back and the blue returns, with the test tube getting warm.

The same reaction, run in both directions, which is what the double arrow means. It is also why anhydrous copper sulfate is used as a **test for water**: if the white powder goes blue, water is present. A reversible reaction is not a failed reaction — here it is the whole point of the substance.

equations.name: Heated one way, watered the other

visual.alt: The reversible equation for hydrated copper sulfate: the blue crystals give white anhydrous copper sulfate and water when heated, and the blue returns when water is added

examples.title: Why a fizzy drink goes flat
examples.body:
A sealed bottle is a closed system, and inside it the carbon dioxide dissolved in the drink is in **equilibrium** with the gas in the space above. High pressure keeps plenty of it dissolved.

Open the bottle and the pressure drops. Le Chatelier says the system will oppose that, and the only way it can raise the pressure is to make more gas — so the dissolved carbon dioxide comes out of solution, which is the hiss and the bubbles. Leave it open and the gas escapes, so the equilibrium never settles and the drink goes flat.

visual.alt: A table comparing a sealed fizzy bottle, where high pressure holds the carbon dioxide in solution at equilibrium, with an opened one, where the pressure falls and the system responds by making more gas until the drink is flat

examples.title: Four ways to push a balance
examples.body:
Every prediction in this topic is the same three steps: name the change, ask how the system can **oppose** it, and read the equation to see which side that means.

That is worth more than four memorised outcomes, because it works on an equation you have never seen. Pressure is the one that needs the equation in front of you: the system moves to the side with **fewer gas molecules**, and if both sides have the same number, pressure does nothing at all.

steps.title: Reversible reactions
steps.body:
In some chemical reactions, **the products of the reaction can react to produce the original reactants**. These are **reversible reactions**, and they are written with a **double arrow**:

$$\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{D}$$

**The direction can be changed by changing the conditions.** The classic demonstration is **hydrated copper(II) sulfate**:

$$\text{hydrated copper sulfate} \rightleftharpoons \text{anhydrous copper sulfate} + \text{water}$$

Heating the **blue** hydrated crystals drives off water and leaves a **white** anhydrous powder. Adding water to the white powder turns it **blue** again, and the reaction gives out heat. Same reaction, two directions, chosen by the conditions.

**Energy changes reverse too.** **If a reversible reaction is exothermic in one direction, it is endothermic in the opposite direction, and the same amount of energy is transferred in each case.**

So if the forward reaction releases $92\text{ kJ}$, the reverse reaction **absorbs** exactly $92\text{ kJ}$. Not more, not less — the same number with the opposite sign.

**Ammonium chloride** is another example: heating it decomposes it into ammonia and hydrogen chloride, which recombine on cooling.

steps.title: What equilibrium means
steps.body:
**When a reversible reaction occurs in apparatus which prevents the escape of reactants and products, equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate.**

Every word of that matters.

**A closed system.** Nothing can get in or out. If a gas escaped, the reverse reaction would lose its supply and the system could never balance.

**Equal rates, not equal amounts.** At equilibrium the forward reaction is still happening, and so is the reverse — at the **same rate**, so the amounts stop changing. This is called a **dynamic** equilibrium: busy, but with no net change.

**How it develops.** At the start there are only reactants, so the forward rate is high and the reverse rate is zero. As products build up, the forward rate **falls** and the reverse rate **rises**. When the two meet, equilibrium has been reached.

**A common misconception**: equilibrium does *not* mean half reactants and half products. The position can lie far to one side. A reaction at equilibrium with 95% products and 5% reactants is just as much at equilibrium as one at 50:50 — what matters is that the proportions have **stopped changing**.

steps.title: Le Chatelier's principle
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)*

**The relative amounts of all the reactants and products at equilibrium depend on the conditions of the reaction.** Change a condition and the system moves to a new equilibrium position.

**Le Chatelier's principle**: **if a system is at equilibrium and a change is made to any of the conditions, then the system responds to counteract the change.**

That single sentence predicts all three effects.

**Concentration.** If the concentration of one of the reactants or products is changed, the system is **no longer at equilibrium** and the concentrations of all the substances change until equilibrium is reached again.

- **Increase a reactant** → **more products** are formed until equilibrium is reached again.
- **Decrease a product** → **more reactants react** until equilibrium is reached again.

**Temperature.** The system counteracts a temperature change by absorbing or releasing heat.

- **Increase** the temperature → the amount of products **increases** for an **endothermic** reaction, and **decreases** for an **exothermic** one.
- **Decrease** the temperature → the opposite in each case.

**Pressure** (for **gaseous** reactions only).

- **Increase** in pressure → the equilibrium shifts towards the side with the **smaller number of molecules**, as shown by the symbol equation.
- **Decrease** in pressure → shifts towards the side with the **larger number of molecules**.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Define equilibrium by rates, not amounts.** "The forward and reverse reactions occur at **exactly the same rate**" is the wording. Saying the amounts are equal is wrong, and saying the reactions have stopped is worse.

**Insist on the closed system.** Equilibrium needs apparatus that **prevents the escape of reactants and products**. This is also why the Haber process recycles its unreacted gases rather than venting them.

**Use the principle as a tool, not a slogan.** Name the change, say **how the system can oppose it**, then read the equation. "It shifts right" without the middle step earns little.

**Count molecules from the balancing numbers.** For pressure, $\mathrm{N_2} + 3\mathrm{H_2}$ is **4** molecules against **2**. Count only **gases**, and remember that **equal numbers mean no effect**.

**Get the temperature logic right.** Heating favours the **endothermic** direction, because absorbing heat is how the system opposes being heated. For an exothermic forward reaction that means **less product** — counterintuitive, and heavily examined.

**A catalyst does not move the equilibrium.** It speeds up the forward and reverse reactions **equally**, so equilibrium is reached **sooner** but at the **same position**. This is the question most often got wrong.

**Distinguish position from rate.** Raising the temperature **lowers the yield** of an exothermic reaction but **increases the rate**. Both are true at once, and industrial questions turn on exactly that tension.

**Explain a colour change through the principle.** Adding water to anhydrous copper sulfate shifts the equilibrium towards the hydrated form, so the solid turns blue — the observation and the principle should be linked explicitly.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- In a **reversible reaction** the products can react to re-form the reactants, shown by **⇌**.
- The **direction can be changed by changing the conditions**.
- If a reaction is **exothermic one way it is endothermic the other**, and **the same amount of energy** is transferred each way.
- **Equilibrium** is reached in a **closed system** when the **forward and reverse reactions occur at exactly the same rate**.
- It is **dynamic**: both reactions continue, but the amounts stop changing.
- Equilibrium does **not** mean equal amounts.
- *(HT)* **Le Chatelier's principle**: the system **responds to counteract** any change in conditions.
- **Increase a reactant** → more products. **Decrease a product** → more reactants react.
- **Raise the temperature** → products **increase** for an **endothermic** reaction, **decrease** for an **exothermic** one.
- **Lower the temperature** → the opposite.
- **Raise the pressure** → shifts to the side with **fewer molecules**; **lower it** → to the side with **more**.
- **Equal numbers of molecules** means pressure has **no effect**.
- A **catalyst** changes the **rate**, never the **position**.

questions.prompt: Explain why adding a catalyst does not change the position of an equilibrium.
questions.solution:
A catalyst lowers the activation energy for the **forward and reverse reactions equally**, so it speeds **both** up by the same factor.

The rates therefore become equal at the **same relative amounts** of reactants and products as before. Equilibrium is reached **sooner**, but the **position** — the proportions present at equilibrium — is **unchanged**.

This is why a catalyst improves how quickly a plant produces material, but never how much it can produce per pass.

questions.prompt: Explain why raising the temperature reduces the yield of an exothermic reaction at equilibrium.
questions.solution:
By **Le Chatelier's principle**, the system **counteracts** the increase in temperature by **absorbing** the extra heat.

Absorbing heat means favouring the **endothermic** direction. If the **forward** reaction is exothermic, then the **reverse** is endothermic, so the equilibrium shifts **backwards**, towards the reactants.

The result is **less product** at the new equilibrium — even though the reaction also goes **faster** at the higher temperature. Rate and yield move in opposite directions here, which is why industrial conditions are always a compromise.

questions.prompt: Explain why equilibrium cannot be reached if a gaseous product is allowed to escape.
questions.solution:
The **reverse** reaction needs the **products** to be present. If a gaseous product escapes, it is continually removed, so the reverse rate stays low and **never rises to match** the forward rate.

The system keeps converting reactants into products until the reactants are exhausted — it goes to completion instead of reaching equilibrium. That is why a closed system is part of the definition.

questions.prompt:
The reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ is exothermic in the forward direction.

Using Le Chatelier's principle, explain the effect on the yield of ammonia of (a) increasing the pressure, (b) increasing the temperature, and (c) adding a catalyst. (6 marks)
questions.solution:
**(a) Increasing the pressure.** Counting the gaseous molecules from the balancing numbers: the left has $1 + 3 = \mathbf{4}$ and the right has $\mathbf{2}$. By Le Chatelier's principle the system **counteracts** an increase in pressure by **occupying less space**, which means shifting towards the side with the **smaller number of molecules** — the **right**. So the **yield of ammonia increases**.

**(b) Increasing the temperature.** The system counteracts a rise in temperature by **absorbing** heat, which means favouring the **endothermic** direction. The forward reaction is **exothermic**, so the **reverse** is endothermic and the equilibrium shifts **left**. The **yield of ammonia therefore falls**.

Note that the reaction also goes **faster** at higher temperature, so rate and yield pull in opposite directions — which is why the Haber process uses a compromise temperature rather than the one that maximises either.

**(c) Adding a catalyst.** A catalyst lowers the activation energy for the **forward and reverse reactions equally**, so it increases **both** rates by the same factor. The rates therefore become equal at the **same proportions** as before: equilibrium is reached **more quickly**, but the **position is unchanged** and the **yield is exactly the same**. A catalyst makes a plant produce ammonia sooner, never more of it per pass.

examTechnique.body:
Define equilibrium by **equal rates** in a **closed system**, not by equal amounts. Then apply **Le Chatelier's principle** in three steps: name the change, say **how the system opposes it**, and read the equation for the direction.

For **pressure**, count gaseous molecules from the balancing numbers — fewer molecules wins at high pressure, and **equal numbers mean no effect**. For **temperature**, heating favours the **endothermic** direction. A **catalyst** never moves the position.
examinerErrors: Omitting the closed system from the definition.
Claiming higher pressure always shifts to the right.
Predicting a pressure shift when both sides have equal molecules.
Saying heating increases the yield of an exothermic reaction.
Claiming a catalyst increases the yield.
Stating a shift without saying how the system opposes the change.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer defines equilibrium by equal **rates** in a **closed system** and explains why both conditions are needed. It applies Le Chatelier's principle as a three-step argument rather than a slogan, counts gaseous molecules from the balancing numbers and spots the equal-molecule case where pressure has no effect, and gets the temperature logic right — heating favours the endothermic direction, so an exothermic reaction yields less. It separates **position** from **rate**, and states firmly that a catalyst shortens the time to equilibrium without moving it.
